messages.subject: Obtaining permutation-adjusted scanone() p-values for all markers, not just for each chromosome's top hit
messages.subject_clean: Obtaining permutation-adjusted scanone() p-values for all markers, not just for each chromosome's top hit
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am calculating permutation-based adjusted P values for my scanone() results.  I would like to obtain the adjusted p-values for all markers, but the summary.scanone() function only provides the adjusted p-value for each chromosome's top-ranked marker.

My goal with this information is to generate plots of adjusted-pvalues along the chromosomes, similar to how plot.scanone does using the raw LOD scores.  An example plot would be Fig2 of Broman (2003 Genetics).

Is it possible to do this?  I took a stab at editing the summary.scanone() function's code but these efforts failed.

Many thanks!
C

PS-My apologies if the answer to this question is already on the board; I searched but couldn't find what I was looking for.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Obtaining permutation-adjusted scanone() p-values for all markers, not just for each chromosome's top hit
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Obtaining permutation-adjusted scanone() p-values for all markers, not just for each chromosome's top hit
messages.body_plain:
You can trick summary to give you p-values for all positions by changing the "chr" column to have a different chromosome ID for each position.

Here's an example:

  library(qtl)
  data(fake.bc)
  fake.bc <- calc.genoprob(fake.bc, step=1)
  out <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk")
  operm <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk", n.perm=1000)

  out_wpval <- out
  out_wpval$chr <- factor(1:nrow(out))
  sum_wpval <- summary(out_wpval, perms=operm, pvalues=TRUE)
  out_wpval$pval <- sum_wpval$pval
  out_wpval$chr <- out$chr

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Understanding the math in est.rf
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

Thanks so much, that's incredibly helpful.

Best,

Joanna

On Tuesday, January 31, 2017 at 1:06:39 AM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
> It'd probably take me longer to find a good explanation than to just try to explain it myself, so here goes:
>
> Consider a backcross (AxB)xA, so that offspring have genotypes AA or AB.
> Let r = recombination fraction between two markers.
>
> There are four possible two-locus genotypes for the pair of markers:
>    parental types: AA/AA, AB/AB   frequency (1-r)/2 each
>    recombinants:   AA/AB, AB/AA   frequency r/2 each
>
> Suppose in data on n individuals, you observe x recombinants and (n-x) non-recombinants.
>
> The log likelihood is then
>
>    l(r) = (n-x) log (1-r) + x log r + constant
>
> The maximum likelihood estimate for r is rhat = x/n.
>
> The log likelihood ratio for the testing the null hypothesis H0:r = 1/2 is then
>
>    l(rhat) - l(1/2) = (n-x) log(1 - x/n) + x log(x/n) - n log(1/2)
>
> Make those logs base 10, and you've got the LOD score.
>
> In an intercross, you can't get a closed-form solution for the MLE, and so we use an EM algorithm.
>
> karl
>
>
> > On Jan 30, 2017, at 4:30 PM, Joanna R. <joanna...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi again,
> >
> > I'm confused about how the LOD scores are filled in in the rf matrix. I understand that to get the recombination frequencies one can either count the recombination events or implement an EM algorithm in more complicated crosses, but how are the LOD scores testing whether rf=0 calculated and added?
> >
> > Thanks so much,
> >
> > Joanna Rifkin
> > PhD candidate
> > Duke University

messages.body_plain:

Now, I don't know which SNPs should be considered for analysis.
I have to discard SNPs those are 'homo (parent1) & homo (parent2)? I have done filtering for hetero (P1) x homo (P2); homo (P1) x hetero (P2) and hetero (P1) x hetero (P2). After filtering, the total number of SNPs is 1651. Should I consider only these SNPs for mapping RIL population?

Please help me with your inputs. I'm doing the analysis for the first time. Also I'm using R first time. I'll highly appreciate your help.

I'm attaching my entire data for any help [https://www.dropbox.com/sh/og2pbp7i6c55ljg/AADwovhNmWRKYNK2iHmkwX2oa?dl=0].

Regards,
Som

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Puzzled!! how to filter the data??
messages.body_plain:
I would start by focusing on the progeny genotypes: omit markers that are monomorphic, or nearly monomorphic.

I only have experience with RIL where the parents are inbred lines. I'm not sure immediately what to do with the case that the parents have heterozygosity. The simplest case to focus on is where the two parents are homozygous with different alleles, so you might just start with those markers.

But are these RIL? My initial impression is that there's quite a lot of heterozygosity in the progeny lines. And segregation distortion.

karl

messages.subject: How to import haploid data
messages.body_plain:
I got the following question; I thought it and my response might be helpful.

> I am planning to use Rqtl for my research project and need some help with the data import. I work on a haploid organism and have an F1 generation from this cross. How would I define the genotypes and alleles for import if it's haploid? Should I just convert them to homozygous diploid genotypes? And do you have a suggestion what would be the best cross type to define for this study as it doesn't correspond to an F1 population of diploid organisms?
>
> Also, I have tried to read extensively through the tutorial and website information but not sure if I understand correctly. Can I use Rqtl to construct my linkage map if the only input data I have is the SNP markers and their chromosome number and position for each individual? I have phenotype data but will do QTL analysis later, initially I just want to construct the map without phenotype data.
>
> Thank you in advance!

You can code genotypes as A/B. There's a cross type "haploid" that would be appropriate.

When importing the data with read.cross, you could do something like:

 mycross <- read.cross("csv", file="my_data.csv", genotypes=c("A","B"), crosstype="haploid")

You need to include at least one "phenotype", but it could just be a sample ID. But then the phenotypes don't much get in the way of the linkage map construction process, so it doesn't hurt to include them.

karl

On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 7:06:29 AM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
write.cross with format="mapqtl" only works for phase-known 4-way cross data.

Your call to read.cross isn't really working properly. The genotypes vector for a 4-way cross needs to be a specific list of genotype codes, corresponding to these:
1 = AC, 2 = BC, 3 = AD, 4 = BD,
5 = A = AC or AD, 6 = B = BC or BD, 7 = C = AC or BC, 8 = D = AD or BD,
9 = AC or BD, 10 = AD or BC,
11 = not AC, 12 = not BC, 13 = not AD, 14 = not BD

So the data object in R is not really what you want, and while it thinks this is a 4-way cross, R/qtl can't convert it into the MapQTL format.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] linkage map with physical distance (bp) in rice
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] linkage map with physical distance (bp) in rice
messages.body_plain:
For QTL mapping, you need cM locations of markers. You can try using estimates based on the Mbp locations in a physical map, using an estimate of the cM/Mbp ratio.

The warning about chromosomes >1000 cM in length is to avoid a common downstream problem that occurs if the marker map is in basepairs: If you run calc.genoprob with step=1, you'd then try to calculate genotype probabilities at every basepair, which is going to cause memory problems.

karl
